extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematical writers (students, researchers, and authors preparing papers or books)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing, editing, and preparing mathematical papers and books, covering proofreading, sentence/notation style, document logistics, and practical drafting habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading (multiple focused passes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreading is essential and should consist of several distinct passes rather than a single quick scan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Suggested passes (verbatim list):
One proofreading should be to check spelling and simple syntax errors (software can help with the former, and even with the latter—see Section 6.4).
One proofreading should be for accuracy.
One proofreading should be for organization and for logic.
One proofreading should be for sense, and for the flow of the ideas.
One proofreading should be for sound.
One proofreading should be for overall coherence.
Also: Paul Halmos said he never published a word before he had read it six times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud to check sound and sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading your work aloud reveals problems of sense, flow, and sound and helps develop an 'ear' for good prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and notes: Laurence Olivier rehearsed by speaking aloud; the author recommends reading mathematics aloud to pick out offending passages quickly. Reading aloud helps to fix alliteration, repetition, awkward constructions, and to ensure sentences flow as conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose precise, elegant terminology and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Select names, terminology, and notation carefully — precise and memorable terms aid communication and long-term reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'continuous' is a perfect name versus 'non-hypererratic'; names influence perception of a concept. The author urges striving for precision and elegance when creating terminology, definitions, and titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context and narrative rather than terse statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer telling the reader what is going on (history, contributors, context) instead of terse, bald statements that lack content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasted passages: a bare statement 'The conjecture of Gauss (1830) is false.' versus a contextual paragraph describing who worked on it, why, and how it was resolved. The latter 'puts the entire matter in context' and 'tells the reader who worked on the conjecture and why.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, empty phrasing; prefer substantive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on vacuous intensifiers or filler; use meaningful content and specific technical facts instead of words like 'very' or empty praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Replace 'This is a very important operator, that has very specific properties, culminating in a very significant theorem.' with contentful phrasing that states the spectral/smoothing properties and the theorem they lead to. Rule of thumb: avoid 'very' unless you'd be comfortable saying 'damn' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition of words/sounds and intrusive alliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not repeat descriptive words or similar sounds in close proximity; avoid forced alliteration which distracts in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: don't use the same word or sound in two consecutive sentences; avoid alliterative constructions like 'semisimple, sesquilinear ... sequenced' that make the reader pause and suspect parody. Use syntactic rephrasing to break up alliteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer short, simple declarative sentences; break up compound/run-on sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical prose is most effective when linking sentences are simple and declarative; break long compound sentences into clearer shorter ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Replace 'As we let x become closer and closer to 0, then y tends ever closer to t0.' with 'When x is close to 0 then y is close to t0.' Also transform long hypothesis-conclusion run-ons into sequences of 'Let'/'Suppose' sentences followed by the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active voice generally; use passive voice only when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Active voice is usually clearer because it identifies the agent; passive voice is acceptable when emphasis on the patient or a stylistic nuance is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Prefer 'The Lie group G acts on the manifold M' over 'The manifold M is acted upon by the Lie group G.' Passive voice can be used if you intentionally want to stress the manifold M rather than G. 'No rule of writing is unbreakable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan, minimize, and be economical with notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid introducing unnecessary notation, avoid starting sentences with symbols, plan notation in advance, and keep notation consistent throughout the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: don't begin clauses with symbols like 'f is said to be...' — prefer 'A function f is said to be...'; avoid phrases like 'Every real, nonsquare x < 0 . . .' which are ambiguous; try to reuse notation consistently across sections; avoid reassigning the same symbol to different meanings (e.g., i as index vs imaginary unit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overuse symbolic notation in prose; prefer English where helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: While notation is powerful, overuse can hinder comprehension; translate key ideas into clear English prose when it improves readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Instead of using many symbols '⇒ ≡ ∋ ∀ ∃' prefer natural language: 'Every nonnegative real number has a square root.' Use symbols where concise clarity is preserved, but avoid excessive symbolic density in sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit with logical connectives and sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Make logical structure clear (use 'then' after 'if', avoid beginning sentences awkwardly with 'if and only if'), and express hypotheses/conclusions unambiguously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'If x > 4, ... then the circle can be squared.' or better 'Suppose x > 4, ... Then the circle can be squared.' Avoid beginning sentences with 'If and only if ...' which is hard to read; consider 'iff' or equivalent rephrasings and use 'then' as a sign post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering system: be consistent and not excessive
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a sensible numbering scheme for pages and displayed items; use it consistently; avoid numbering everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options: number all displayed items sequentially across a chapter (e.g., '3.6.4' for 4th displayed item in section 6 of chapter 3) or number items within sections. Use a consistent scheme so the reader can find things easily. Do not number every paragraph or every formula — only what you will refer to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include identifying metadata on drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even drafts should include author name, date, affiliation, and contact information so they can be identified and traced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put your name on every draft, a date (or time), affiliation (e.g., Harvard or visiting institution), and an email address so collaborators or readers can find you if the draft circulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting habits and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use practical physical habits and materials (write on one side of paper, use readable pens, leave space, write large and double-spaced) to ease editing and later typesetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: write on one side of the paper only (allows side-by-side comparison), use black ink/fountain or roller pens that don't smear, discard pens that blot, double or triple space for editorial insertions, use colored pens for notes, keep supplies (Wite-Out, Post-it, stapler, dictionary) at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize your workspace and protect writing time
rubrics_metrics.description: Write where you can concentrate without interruption and protect writing intervals; minimize clutter and separate eating/drinking areas to prevent accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations: close the door, unplug the phone, have food on a separate side table, keep desk free of clutter to avoid accidents (coffee spills), and find a place/schedule where you can get into the flow (may take up to an hour to warm up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography and reference management
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep organized, informal reference notes while drafting and defer assembling formal bibliographic data until after writing; use tools like LaTeX and MathSciNet to assemble references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: assign short acronyms (e.g., [GH]) to references during drafting and keep a sheet listing them; compile full bibliographic entries after finishing the text; LaTeX and online services (MathSciNet, library catalogs) help automate bibliography assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain writing momentum; postpone lookups until later
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not interrupt productive writing flow to look up references or details; mark notes to yourself and continue writing so you take advantage of the writing moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: when you need to look something up (a theorem, a reference), make a red-pen note such as 'find this reference' or 'fill this gap' but keep writing. Interruptions to the library or web search break productive momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use typographic conventions when defining or referring to terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a term, italicize it; when referring to a word as an object, put it in quotation marks for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'We call Γ the fundamental solution for the partial differential operator L.' Italicize the term at first definition and use quotes when discussing the word itself (e.g., put 'the' in quotes when discussing the definite article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word order and punctuation affect clarity; avoid comma overuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Word order subtly alters emphasis or meaning; commas indicate logical pauses and should not be overused or arbitrarily inserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: different word order in 'Yellow is the color of my true love's hair' vs 'My true love's hair has the color yellow' emphasizes different aspects. Avoid sentences with gratuitous commas like 'We went to the store, to buy some potatoes.' Read aloud to detect awkward comma usage and illogical pauses.
